summary: Alf Sommerfelt (1892–1965) was a linguist who founded the Norwegian Association for Linguistics in 1924. He served as professor of linguistics at the University of Oslo from 1931 to 1962 and taught André Padoux.

Alf Torp (1853–1916) was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He studied at Oslo under Sophus Bugge and Leipzig under Ernst Windisch and Georg Curtius, later serving as professor of Sanskrit and comparative linguistics at Oslo (1894–1914).

Alfons Fürst (b. 1961) works in religious studies and history/archaeology. He studied under Richard von Garbe, at Tübingen, and at Regensburg. He held a chair substitution at Bamberg (~2001–2002) and became a professor at Münster in 2000.

Alfons Hilka (1877–1939) worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Breslau under Carl Appel and Alfred Hillebrandt, and at Berlin under Adolf Tobler. He was a professor at Greifswald (1918) and Göttingen (1921).

Alfons Klaus Weidert (1943–1988) was a linguist and Tibetologist. He earned his Ph.D. at Heidelberg University (~1966–1971), held a research position at the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (~1977–1984), and was a Privatdozent at Kiel University in 1982.

Alfons Nehring (1890–1967) was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Berlin and Breslau under Otto Schrader. He taught at Breslau, held professorships at Würzburg (1930; 1952–1958), and was an associate professor at Marquette (1938) and Fordham (1943).

Alfons Väth (1874–1937) was an Indologist and historian. He founded St. Xavier's College, Mumbai, in 1913, where he taught English and Indian history (~1911–1914), and later served as editor of Die Katholischen Missionen (1918–1925).

Alfonsa Ferrari (1918–1954) was a scholar of Tibetology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. She studied under Carlo Formichi, Giuseppe Tucci, Theodor Bloch, Louis Renou, Jacques Bacot, and Marcelle Lalou, and became professor of Sanskrit at Sapienza University of Rome in 1951.

Alfred Bloch (1915–1983) was a linguist and Indologist. He earned his Ph.D. at the University of Basel (1933–1939), where he later served as Privatdozent (1942) and as instructor for Indo-European linguistics and Hebrew lecturer (1949–1982).

Alfred Bloom (1926–2017) was a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Japanology. Educated at Harvard under Masatoshi Nagatomi, among other institutions, he was professor of religion at Oregon (1961–1970) and dean at the Institute of Buddhist Studies (1986–1994).

Alfred Chilton Pearson (1861–1935) was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He received his education at King's College School, Highgate School, and Christ's College, Cambridge, where he studied under John Peile.

Alfred Cooper Woolner (1878–1936) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Trinity College, Oxford, under Arthur Anthony Macdonell. He served as principal of Oriental College (from 1903) and dean of university instruction at University of the Punjab (1903–1936).

Alfred Cort Haddon (1855–1940) studied at King's College London and Christ's College, Cambridge. He held academic posts at the University of Cambridge (1879–1880, 1900–1926) and the Royal College of Science for Ireland (1880–1901).
Alfred Darby was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at St Augustine's College, Canterbury, and earned a B.D. from Durham University in 1908, later holding a post at Rajaram College.

Alfred Edward Housman (1859–1936) worked in linguistics and other fields. He studied at King Edward's School, Bromsgrove School, and St John's College, Oxford, and later held a post at University College London (~1892–1911).

Alfred Ernout (1879–1973) was a linguist who studied under Antoine Meillet at the Sorbonne and EPHE. He held professorships at the University of Lille, EPHE, the University of Paris, and Collège de France (1944–1951).

Alfred Forke (1867–1944) was a scholar of Sinology and philosophy. He studied under Carl Arendt, whom he succeeded at the Seminar for Oriental Languages in 1903. He later served as professor of Chinese at the University of Hamburg (1923–1935).

Alfred Foucher (1865–1952) was a scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and archaeology. He studied under Sylvain Lévi at EPHE, served as professor at the University of Paris (1907; 1929–1936), and directed the Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan (1922–1925).

Alfred Gell (1945–1997) studied at the University of Cambridge under Edmund Leach and at the London School of Economics. He subsequently held lecturer posts at the University of Sussex (1972–1974), Australian National University (1974–1979), and LSE (1979–1997).

Alfred Hillebrandt (1853–1927) was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler at Breslau and Martin Haug at Munich. He spent his career at the University of Breslau, where he became a full professor in 1887.
